title: MiniMax Learning of Interpretable Factored Stochastic Policies from Conjoint Data, with Uncertainty Quantification
claim: Estimator error shrinks with sample size and stays stable across population composition, while interval coverage stays near nominal.

description: Two side-by-side line charts in grayscale, both with the proportion of Republican voters (0.2 to 0.8) on the x-axis. The left panel, titled 'RMSE of π̂_R', shows three lines for sample sizes 1000 (light gray), 5000 (medium gray) and 10000 (black). RMSE falls clearly as sample size grows, from about 0.14 to 0.06 to 0.045. The curves are mostly flat, with slight U-shapes. The right panel, titled 'Coverage Probability for π_R', plots coverage on a 0 to 1 axis. All three lines sit near 0.95, with the n=1000 line dipping to about 0.87 to 0.90 at the extremes. Each panel has its own legend on the right. The eye goes first to the widely separated RMSE curves on the left.

abstract: We study offline policy optimization over exponentially large factorial action spaces from randomized preference data, showing how conjoint experiments can estimate interpretable stochastic policies with asymptotically valid uncertainty under regularity conditions. Conjoint analyses typically report Average Marginal Component Effects (AMCEs) by averaging over opponent attributes and thus ignore strategic interdependence. We instead learn stochastic interventions -- product-of-Categorical policies over factor levels -- that (i) optimize expected outcomes in an average-case setting and (ii) extend to a two-player minimax (adversarial) setting that realistically captures simultaneous strategic candidate selection. Methodologically, we derive a closed-form optimizer for a tractable two-way interaction regime with L2 variance regularization, and provide a general gradient-based procedure for richer model classes. Uncertainty from the outcome model propagates asymptotically to both the optimal policy and its value via a Delta method approximation. We further model institutional details (e.g., primaries) inside the minimax objective and introduce a data-driven measure of strategic divergence between parties. On synthetic data, we empirically characterize finite-sample error and coverage as dimensionality and $n$ vary. On a U.S. presidential conjoint, adversarially learned policies produce restricted-equilibrium vote shares that align with historical election ranges in our data, in stark contrast to non-adversarial (averaging) optimizers.
